issues.description: Use of Object.hasOwn() may not be supported in older JavaScript environments
issues.suggestion: Consider using 'value in WEIGHTS' or add a polyfill for broader compatibility. Alternatively, use 'Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(WEIGHTS, value)' for maximum safety against prototype pollution, though Object.hasOwn is the modern preferred approach if targeting ES2022+.

issues.description: comparePriority assumes valid Priority types but doesn't validate input
issues.suggestion: Add defensive validation or document that callers must ensure valid priorities. Consider: 'export function comparePriority(a, b) { if (!isPriority(a) || !isPriority(b)) { throw new TypeError("Invalid priority"); } return WEIGHTS[b] - WEIGHTS[a]; }' for production robustness.

issues.description: Array spread and sort creates a new array which is correct, but could document the O(n log n) complexity
issues.suggestion: This is actually good practice (non-mutating). For very large arrays (>10k items), consider documenting performance characteristics or providing a mutating variant if needed. Current implementation is optimal for typical use cases.

issues.description: toPriority silently coerces invalid values to DEFAULT_PRIORITY without notification
issues.suggestion: Consider logging a warning for invalid priorities in development mode to help catch bugs: 'export function toPriority(value) { if (!isPriority(value) && process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production") { console.warn(`Invalid priority: ${value}, using default`); } return isPriority(value) ? value : DEFAULT_PRIORITY; }'

issues.description: Nested toPriority calls in sort comparator are safe but could be optimized for large datasets
issues.suggestion: For arrays with thousands of items, consider memoizing or pre-processing: 'export function sortByPriority(todos) { return [...todos].sort((a, b) => { const aPrio = toPriority(a.priority); const bPrio = toPriority(b.priority); return WEIGHTS[bPrio] - WEIGHTS[aPrio]; }); }' This avoids repeated lookups, though the current implementation is clean and likely sufficient.

codeQuality.summary: Excellent code quality with modern JavaScript patterns and strong type safety via JSDoc. The file demonstrates best practices: immutable data structures (Object.freeze), proper type guards (isPriority), non-mutating operations (sortByPriority), and defensive programming (toPriority fallback). No security vulnerabilities detected. The code is well-documented, uses modern ES2022 features appropriately, and follows functional programming principles. Minor improvements could include additional validation in comparePriority and development-mode warnings for invalid inputs. Overall, this is production-ready code with solid architecture.

untestedPaths.reasoning: No test verifies behavior when todos array contains invalid priority values (not just missing). If a.priority or b.priority is an invalid string like 'URGENT' or 'medium', toPriority will coerce to 'normal', potentially causing unexpected sort behavior.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('sortByPriority handles invalid priority values by treating them as default', () => { const sorted = sortByPriority([{ priority: 'low' }, { priority: 'INVALID' }, { priority: 'urgent' }]); assert.deepEqual(sorted.map(t => t.priority), ['urgent', 'INVALID', 'low']); assert.equal(sorted[1].priority, 'INVALID'); });

untestedPaths.reasoning: No test verifies stable sort behavior when multiple todos have the same priority. JavaScript's Array.sort() is stable as of ES2019, but this critical behavior for user experience isn't explicitly tested.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('sortByPriority maintains stable sort for same priority', () => { const sorted = sortByPriority([{ id: 1, priority: 'high' }, { id: 2, priority: 'high' }, { id: 3, priority: 'high' }]); assert.deepEqual(sorted.map(t => t.id), [1, 2, 3]); });

untestedPaths.reasoning: No test covers todos with non-string but truthy priority values (e.g., numbers, objects, arrays). The toPriority function expects unknown but sortByPriority doesn't document this edge case.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('sortByPriority handles non-string priority values', () => { const sorted = sortByPriority([{ priority: 123 }, { priority: 'urgent' }, { priority: {} }]); assert.deepEqual(sorted.map(t => typeof t.priority === 'string' ? t.priority : 'coerced'), ['urgent', 'coerced', 'coerced']); });

untestedPaths.reasoning: No test verifies behavior with string subclasses or String objects (new String('low')). While unlikely in practice, Object.hasOwn might behave unexpectedly with boxed strings.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('isPriority handles String objects correctly', () => { assert.equal(isPriority(new String('low')), false); assert.equal(isPriority(Object('high')), false); });

untestedPaths.reasoning: No test verifies behavior with a single-item array. While trivial, it's a boundary condition that should be covered for completeness.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('sortByPriority handles single item array', () => { const sorted = sortByPriority([{ priority: 'low' }]); assert.deepEqual(sorted, [{ priority: 'low' }]); });

untestedPaths.reasoning: No test verifies all possible priority combinations. Currently only tests 3 cases (urgent>low, low<urgent, high==high) but there are 16 possible combinations (4x4 matrix).
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('comparePriority handles all priority combinations correctly', () => { const priorities = ['low', 'normal', 'high', 'urgent']; for (let i = 0; i < priorities.length; i++) { for (let j = 0; j < priorities.length; j++) { const result = comparePriority(priorities[i], priorities[j]); if (i === j) assert.equal(result, 0); else if (i < j) assert.ok(result > 0); else assert.ok(result < 0); } } });

untestedPaths.reasoning: No explicit test for passing DEFAULT_PRIORITY itself to toPriority(). While covered indirectly, explicit testing ensures the default is itself a valid priority.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('toPriority accepts DEFAULT_PRIORITY as valid input', () => { assert.equal(toPriority(DEFAULT_PRIORITY), DEFAULT_PRIORITY); });

untestedPaths.reasoning: No test verifies behavior with extremely large arrays (performance edge case). While not a functional bug, sorting large todo lists should not cause performance issues.
untestedPaths.suggestedTest: test('sortByPriority handles large arrays efficiently', () => { const large = Array.from({ length: 10000 }, (_, i) => ({ priority: PRIORITIES[i % 4] })); const start = Date.now(); const sorted = sortByPriority(large); const elapsed = Date.now() - start; assert.ok(elapsed < 100, 'Should sort 10k items in <100ms'); assert.equal(sorted.length, 10000); });

testCoverage.summary: The test file src/utils/priority.test.js provides good baseline coverage with 13 tests covering all 4 exported functions, 2 constants, and basic edge cases. However, 75% estimated coverage leaves gaps in several important areas: (1) HIGH priority - sortByPriority doesn't test invalid (but non-missing) priority values being coerced to default; (2) MEDIUM priority - no tests for stable sort behavior with duplicate priorities, non-string priority values, or large array performance; (3) LOW priority - missing tests for String objects, single-item arrays, exhaustive comparePriority combinations, and DEFAULT_PRIORITY validation. The existing tests are well-written and cover the happy path plus common edge cases (null/undefined, empty arrays, mutation prevention, inherited properties). Adding the suggested 8 tests would bring coverage to ~95% and significantly improve confidence in edge case handling.

suggestions.description: Replace Object.keys() with Object.entries() and map to avoid type casting
suggestions.benefits: Removes unnecessary type casting. Object.keys() already returns string[], and TypeScript/JSDoc can infer this correctly. The explicit cast adds complexity without value.

suggestions.description: Use Map instead of frozen object for better semantic clarity and performance
suggestions.benefits: Map provides better semantics for key-value lookups, has built-in .has() method (more semantic than Object.hasOwn), and slightly better performance for frequent lookups. It's also inherently iterable.

suggestions.description: Update isPriority to use Map.has() if Map is adopted
suggestions.benefits: More semantic and clearer intent. Map.has() is purpose-built for checking key existence, whereas Object.hasOwn() is a workaround for object-based lookups.

suggestions.description: Extract priority extraction logic to reduce nested function calls
suggestions.benefits: Improves readability by breaking down complex nested calls. Also potentially improves performance by avoiding duplicate function calls if the sort algorithm makes multiple comparisons with the same elements.

suggestions.location: Lines 23, 38, 51, 60: Consolidate into a Priority class
suggestions.description: Encapsulate priority logic in a class for better organization and extensibility
suggestions.benefits: Encapsulates all priority-related logic in a single cohesive unit. Uses private static fields (#WEIGHTS) to prevent external modification. Provides a clear namespace and makes the module easier to extend (e.g., adding priority colors, icons, etc.). Maintains backward compatibility with existing exports.

refactorings.summary: The code is already well-written with modern patterns like const, Object.freeze(), and JSDoc types. Key improvements include: (1) migrating from frozen objects to Map for better semantics and performance, (2) reducing nested function calls in sortByPriority for clarity, (3) optionally consolidating into a PriorityHandler class for better encapsulation and extensibility. The class-based approach (suggestion #8) provides the highest impact by creating a single source of truth for priority logic and using private fields for true immutability. All suggestions maintain or improve type safety and code clarity.

testCoverage.summary: The test suite for priority.test.js is well-structured with good coverage of core functionality (85%). It properly tests all exported functions, handles prototype pollution, validates immutability, and covers basic edge cases. However, it misses several important edge cases: whitespace handling in isPriority (medium priority), mixed-case input validation (high priority), comprehensive comparePriority combinations (medium priority), and DEFAULT_PRIORITY validation (medium priority). The tests follow modern Node.js test patterns using node:test and assert/strict, which is excellent. Recommended additions focus on input validation edge cases, sort stability, and ensuring the DEFAULT_PRIORITY constant is valid. No critical security or data-loss paths are present in this utility module, so missing tests are primarily medium-to-low priority improvements for robustness.

recommendations.description: Add test cases for mixed-case priority values ('High', 'Normal', 'Urgent', 'LOW') to verify case sensitivity is enforced. These are common user input patterns that should be explicitly rejected.
Add explicit test for invalid priority values in sortByPriority to verify they are coerced to DEFAULT_PRIORITY during sorting. Current tests only cover missing (undefined) priorities.
Consider migrating from Object.freeze() with object literals to Map for WEIGHTS. Map provides better semantics, built-in .has() method, and improved performance for lookups.
Fix test assertion on line 56-58 that uses nullish coalescing (??), which masks whether sortByPriority preserves undefined or converts it. Test should verify actual undefined value explicitly.
Organize test file with describe() blocks to group tests by function (isPriority, toPriority, comparePriority, sortByPriority) for better structure and readability.
Add tests for sort stability (multiple items with same priority), comprehensive comparePriority combinations, and DEFAULT_PRIORITY validation.
Object.hasOwn() requires ES2022+. Consider adding a polyfill or using Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call() for broader browser compatibility.
Add development-mode warnings in toPriority() when invalid priorities are coerced to DEFAULT_PRIORITY to help developers catch bugs early.
Extract priority extraction logic in sortByPriority to reduce nested function calls and improve readability. Store toPriority results in variables before passing to comparePriority.
